claims.statement: IMDT's stated route to its dog trainer qualification is a 2-day theory course, a 4-day practical course and a membership assessment; the 2-day and 4-day courses each cover half of the curriculum for the OCN Level 3 'Principles of Dog Training and Behaviour' qualification, and further correspondence courses at Levels 3 to 5 lead towards behaviourist membership.
claims.locator: What courses do I need to do
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: 2-day theory, 4-day practical, assessment; courses can be taken in any order.
claims.confidenceJustification: Stated on IMDT's own pages (how-to-become and 2-day course page).
limitations: Describes IMDT's trainer pathway, not an owner curriculum.

claims.statement: The IMDT 2-day course outline lists the science of how dogs learn, body language, group class planning and dynamics, principles of canine behaviour, building a one-to-one consultation, and behaviour modification and rehabilitation.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Six headline topics for the theory course.
claims.confidenceJustification: Outline read directly from the course page.
limitations: Headings only; course content is not public.

claims.statement: The IMDT 4-day practical course outline covers coaching exercises, methods and exercises to teach in class, observational skills, class planning, layout and dynamics, applying learning theory to practical classes, and teaching real people with real dogs; about 80 per cent is hands-on practical work outdoors.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Practical coaching and class-planning course, mostly hands-on.
claims.confidenceJustification: Outline read directly from the course page.

claims.statement: IMDT lists the knowledge a qualified trainer needs as how dogs learn, canine body language and behaviour, observational skills, motivating dog and owner, positive-reinforcement-based training, planning classes, assessing a dog and structuring a one-to-one session, communicating with owners, and practical work with different dogs and real owners.
claims.locator: What does a dog training qualification cover?
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Eleven knowledge areas for a qualified trainer.

claims.statement: IMDT's practical assessment (v26.1) asks the candidate to coach one of twelve exercises: emergency stop, mat target, send around, down, middle, chin rest, nose to hand touch, twist or spin, recall, loose lead walking, muzzle training and retrieve; marks cover a brief consultation, management and safety, communication, practical training (the largest share) and follow-up questions.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Twelve assessed exercises; practical training is 31 of 50 marks.
claims.confidenceJustification: Extracted from the PDF text of the current guideline.
limitations: Assesses trainers coaching an assessor, not owners.

claims.statement: IMDT's assessment Q&A (v26.1) marks equipment use and conditioning out of 4, dog law and the Code of Ethics out of 2, body language out of 4, general training knowledge out of 8, operant conditioning out of 16 and classical conditioning out of 16.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Operant and classical conditioning carry 32 of 50 marks.
claims.confidenceJustification: Extracted from the PDF text of the current guideline.

claims.statement: NPSA describes classical conditioning as a dog learning that a neutral stimulus reliably occurs before or with a meaningful stimulus it already responds to, after which the neutral stimulus alone produces a similar response.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Neutral stimulus paired with meaningful stimulus becomes a predictor.

claims.statement: NPSA describes operant conditioning as a dog learning that its own voluntary actions lead to consequences: behaviour followed by something the dog likes becomes stronger, and behaviour followed by something it dislikes becomes weaker; it recommends that training primarily use reward-based methods.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Consequences change the likelihood of repeating behaviour; reward-based approach advised.

claims.statement: NPSA explains that habituation, where a dog stops reacting to something that has no important consequence, works best when many new stimuli are introduced gradually from a young age at low intensity, and that sensitisation, where reactions grow stronger with repeated exposure, can be hard to overcome and may need a certified clinical animal behaviourist.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Gradual low-intensity exposure; sensitisation may need clinical help.
claims.confidenceJustification: Stated explicitly; consistent with Dogs Trust socialisation guidance.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust advises that any dog benefits from being able to wear a muzzle comfortably, for safety when frightened, ill or injured, to stop harmful eating, to protect others, or where the law requires it; the muzzle should let the dog eat, drink and pant (a basket type), fit without obscuring vision or digging in, and a muzzle does not change how the dog feels about a trigger.
claims.locator: Why would my dog need to wear a muzzle?; Choosing a muzzle
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Basket muzzle that allows panting; fit; muzzle does not treat fear.
claims.confidenceJustification: Page fetched in full; agrees with Blue Cross and PDSA.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust teaches muzzle wearing in small steps: let the dog freely put its nose in and out, reward looking at the muzzle, then treats at and inside the opening, then the dog choosing to put its nose in, then slowly building time, adding steps backwards, getting used to the clip sound and loose straps, fastening briefly and unfastening, and only then lengthening wear time with fun activities and short walks; if the dog is unsure the owner goes back to the last relaxed stage.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Voluntary nose-in, then duration, movement, straps, fastening, longer wear.
claims.confidenceJustification: Page fetched in full; explicit sequence.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust says muzzle training by the food method may not suit a dog that guards food or dislikes people near its bowl, or one that struggles with its face being touched, and that such dogs need an accredited behaviourist or the charity's behaviour support line; a dog still frightened of the muzzle should see a vet, and a different style of muzzle should be used for any emergency muzzling during training.
claims.locator: How to train your dog to wear a muzzle; What to do if my dog is worried
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Guarding or face-touch sensitivity: professional help first.
claims.confidenceJustification: Page fetched in full; explicit cautions.

claims.statement: Blue Cross recommends a basket-style muzzle that lets the dog breathe, drink and take treats, notes that muzzles that close the mouth stop panting, advises checking the neck strap allows no more than one small finger, and suggests giving muzzle-training treats only while the muzzle is on so the dog links it with rewards.
claims.locator: What muzzle should you use?; How to make sure a muzzle is a good fit; Step four tip
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Basket style; strap fit; treat only while worn.
claims.confidenceJustification: Page fetched in full; ABTC-CAB behaviourist video on page.

claims.statement: PDSA warns that a muzzle must never be used as punishment, that skipping training and simply putting a muzzle on tends to scare the dog, that a dog must never be left alone wearing one, that mouth-closing muzzles should only be used for a few minutes because they stop panting and drinking, and that flat-faced breeds need vet advice because a muzzle can worsen breathing.
claims.locator: Things to avoid; Which type of muzzle; Muzzling flat-faced breeds
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Never punish, never leave alone, short use only for closed muzzles, vet advice for flat faces.

protocols.title: Teach a dog to wear a basket muzzle comfortably
protocols.intendedOutcome: Dog chooses to put its nose into a well-fitted basket muzzle, accepts the straps, and stays relaxed wearing it for increasing periods.
inappropriateWhen: Dog guards food or dislikes people near its bowl
Dog struggles with its face or head being touched
Flat-faced breed without vet advice on a suitable muzzle
equipment: Small tasty treats or lickable paste
protocols.baselineAssessment: Check the muzzle fits and your dog can eat, drink and pant in it.

steps.instruction: Let your dog see the muzzle and reward every look. Then place treats around and just inside the opening, and let your dog choose to put its nose in and out. Never move the muzzle onto your dog's face.
steps.rewardTiming: Mark and reward each voluntary approach.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog happily puts its nose into the muzzle for treats.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Put the muzzle on the floor and scatter treats near it, moving them closer slowly.
failureModes: Pushing the muzzle towards the dog
Putting it on before the dog is comfortable

steps.instruction: Build time with the nose in by feeding treats or paste through the end, then add one or two steps backwards so your dog follows. Get your dog used to the clip sound and to loose straps at a distance, rewarding calm.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat through the end of the muzzle while the dog stays in.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog stays in the muzzle for several seconds and walks forward with it.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Go back to the last stage where your dog was relaxed and move on more slowly.

steps.instruction: Fasten the clip briefly, reward, and take the muzzle off straight away. Slowly build how long it stays on, and plan a fun activity before it goes on. Later add short quiet walks and other places. Refresh the training every so often.
steps.rewardTiming: Treats only while the muzzle is on.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog stays relaxed wearing the fastened muzzle during short activities.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Shorten wear time; if your dog paws at the muzzle, distract it, remove the muzzle and go back a stage.
failureModes: Leaving the muzzle on too long

protocols.generalisationMaintenance: Practise in new places and refresh regularly, even for dogs who wear a muzzle often.
welfareMonitoring: Dog can pant, drink and eat
Skin is not rubbed or sore
stopConditions: Stop if your dog shows stress or the muzzle rubs. Never leave a muzzled dog alone.
referralRequirements: Accredited behaviourist if your dog guards food, dislikes its face being touched, or stays frightened of the muzzle; your vet for fit advice.
protocols.reviewReason: Muzzle use is safety-adjacent (aggression, pain, breathing in flat-faced breeds). Three consistent charity sources, but wording needs behaviourist review before owner export.

lessons.title: Teach your dog to wear a muzzle happily
lessons.summary: Go slowly, let your dog choose, and make the muzzle mean treats. Never use it as punishment.
